title: Big Ten Unanimously Votes Ban on NFL Players Returning to College; Other Power Four Conferences Follow
dek: The Big Ten unanimously voted Tuesday to ban athletes who have signed professional contracts, been on professional rosters, or declared for the NFL Draft without withdrawing from competing at member schools. The move comes after a Louisiana court granted a temporary restraining order allowing players like Dae'Quan Wright to return to college after participating in NFL preseason. The SEC, ACC, Big 12, and The American are reportedly considering similar rules.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: The Big Ten became the first Power Four conference to vote on a rule prohibiting NFL-contracted players, those with professional roster experience, or underclassmen with unwithdrawn NFL Draft declarations from competing at member institutions.
bottom_line: The Big Ten's preemptive ban signals conference determination to prevent further court-ordered returns, but the Aug. 31 injunction hearing in Louisiana and potential additional lawsuits may test whether the new eligibility rules hold. Watch for whether other Power Four conferences formally adopt similar bans and whether players file separate state lawsuits to challenge the restrictions.
body:
The Big Ten unanimously voted Tuesday to prohibit football players who have signed professional contracts, were on a professional roster at any point, or declared for the NFL Draft as underclassmen without withdrawing from maintaining athletic eligibility at member schools, according to Front Office Sports. The conference became the first among the Power Four to implement such a rule, responding to a legal opening created by a Louisiana court order.
A Louisiana state judge granted a temporary restraining order allowing a group of players who participated in NFL training camp and preseason to return to college competition. Those players, including Cleveland Browns tight end Dae'Quan Wright, were required to terminate their professional contracts and return any money earned while on an NFL preseason roster to qualify. The judge scheduled a hearing for a full injunction on August 31.
Wright has secured a deal to play for LSU after being waived by the Browns, according to Front Office Sports, making him the first player to go from participating in preseason games directly to college competition.
The Big Ten's rule includes specific carve-outs: players who completed four years and were entered into the draft through the automatic entry process (and were not drafted) remain eligible, as do players who participated only in rookie mini-camp tryouts without signing with a team. The distinction reflects an effort to target only players with formal professional standing.
Other conferences are moving to establish similar restrictions. The SEC was holding a meeting Tuesday to discuss eligibility rules, and per Front Office Sports, the conference issued a statement saying that "individuals who choose to leave college athletics, sign professional playing contracts, and compete professionally should not then be permitted to return to college competition." The ACC and Big 12 are reportedly in similar conversations, and The American is considering a conference-wide ban.
LSU coach Lane Kiffin defended signing Wright, saying per Front Office Sports that "because of these rulings, they're either going to play for you, or they're going to play somewhere else around the country. So we made the decision to recruit them, like a lot of other people are." The broader situation carries stakes for the Aug. 31 NFL roster cutdown deadline, when teams must reduce from 90 to 53 players, potentially creating additional eligibility claimants for college.
The NCAA has cautioned against court intervention in eligibility disputes. The organization stated, per Front Office Sports, that "courts across the country granting relief to ineligible athletes who already had every opportunity to compete in college, sometimes without even having a hearing, are failing to appreciate the destabilizing effect their rulings are having on college sports." Sports attorney Darren Heitner reported receiving inquiries from at least a dozen players or their representatives between Wednesday and Monday about filing lawsuits, suggesting the litigation may expand.
